title: Session theft against cloud and EHR browser access
threat: Adversary-in-the-middle phishing and stolen session cookies replayed to read ePHI
vulnerability: Phishable MFA in the assumed current state; the third-party EHR browser path is not enforced by continuous access evaluation, so a stolen session lives until the EHR's own timeout
controls: Phishing-resistant MFA by persona (ADR-003; CA-03, CA-07, CA-11); browser-only session controls on unmanaged devices (PEP-SESSION-PROXY, CA-10); risk-based policies (CA-17, CA-18); token protection on Windows (CA-21); short EHR sessions and sign-in frequency (02 section 9); session-replay detection DX-03, device code and authentication transfer detection SN-04, and mail-hiding and forwarding rule detection DX-04 (untested templates)
notes: The threat model rates AP-1 High likelihood and High impact with the design in place. RR-03 is the open gap.
label: Reference work: fictional scenario, not any organization's risk register

title: Help-desk MFA enrollment fraud followed by payment diversion
threat: Social engineering of the help desk to register an attacker-controlled method, then mailbox access used to divert payer or payroll payments
vulnerability: Help-desk identity checks that rely on knowledge of identifiers; interim methods accepted during the phishing-resistant rollout
controls: In-person or sponsor-verified identity proofing before any method registration (03 section 2); Temporary Access Pass only for registering a phishing-resistant method (CA-19); SMS and voice disabled; SN-01 links an MFA method change to a new-country sign-in or a mail-hiding or forwarding rule within 24 hours, and DX-04 flags mail-hiding and forwarding rules (untested templates); the banking-change link is not built because payer, payroll, and ERP logs are not in Sentinel (A-17); callback verification and dual approval for bank changes (process)
notes: The residual assumes the phishing-resistant rollout is complete. During rollout the threat model rates AP-2 High likelihood.
label: Reference work: fictional scenario, not any organization's risk register

title: Ransomware that stops clinical systems
assets: RES-EHR; RES-PACS; RES-LIS; RES-PHARM; RES-FILES; PEP-HOST; SVC-BACKUP
threat: Ransomware operators move from a phished workstation across the clinical network, impair defenses, destroy recovery points, and encrypt systems
vulnerability: Flat clinical networks and peer-to-peer workstation traffic in the assumed current state; recovery capability unverified: requirements are set (ADR-009), but the implementation is not designed and no restore has been tested
controls: Host east-west blocking (PEP-HOST, WP-2.1); datacenter micro-segmentation (PEP-NET-ZONE, WP-2.2); application control, EDR, and attack disruption (PEP-HOST, PIP-EDR, PIP-XDR); tiering and PAWs (ADR-004); local-first clinical failure modes and downtime procedures (ADR-008); detections for recovery inhibition (DX-01 and SG-01 on Windows hosts, SN-05 for Azure-native backup), mass file renaming (DX-02), workstation-to-workstation SMB and tool transfer (DX-08), endpoint protection tampering (DX-09, SG-02), and Office applications starting script interpreters (SG-03), all untested templates; recovery requirements for SVC-BACKUP (ADR-009: immutable and offline copies, isolation from Tier 0 administrative reach, tested restores with evidence, monitoring as Tier 0), with the implementation not designed
treatment: Mitigate; recovery requirements set (ADR-009); recovery design and restore tests required
notes: Recovery is the decisive control in AP-4. ADR-009 sets its requirements, but a requirement proves nothing, so AP-4's impact band stays Critical (threat-model.md TM-A1), which this register scores as impact 5, Severe (risk-register.md section 5 maps the threat model's bands to this register's scale). Once a data set's copies pass restore tests against ADR-009, the threat model lets AP-4's impact for that data set fall one band and no further: encryption still takes clinical systems offline until restores finish, and data taken before encryption stays taken.
label: Reference work: fictional scenario, not any organization's risk register

title: Compromised partner tenant reaches the EHR or an imaging modality
assets: PEP-VENDOR-BROKER; IDS-PARTNER; IGA-ENTRA; RES-EHR; RES-IOMT; EXT-VENDOR-EHR; EXT-VENDOR-BIOMED; EXT-RCM-BA
threat: An attacker controls a vendor or outsourcer identity that Contoso trusts for MFA claims and uses an approved session to reach EHR systems or, through a biomedical vendor's session (F-07), an imaging modality that holds ePHI
vulnerability: Inbound MFA trust accepts the partner's authentication; vendor VPN with standing access in the assumed current state
controls: Broker-only, recorded vendor sessions (PEP-VENDOR-BROKER, ADR-002); PIM for Groups activation approved by a named Contoso owner (IGA-ENTRA): the system owner for the EHR vendor (F-06), clinical engineering for each biomedical vendor's own session group (F-07); CA-13, CA-14, CA-16; narrow targets through PEP-NET-ZONE, limited for biomedical vendors to that vendor's devices in Z-IOMT-IMAGING; due diligence before inbound trust (A-12); detection of PIM for Groups activations of any vendor session group outside expected hours (SN-02, untested template)
notes: The remaining exposure is an approver who is socially engineered, plus the inbound-trust assumption itself (RR-06). The biomedical vendor variant reaches less data per session than the EHR path, so it does not raise AP-3's rating or these scores. It lands on a medical device (RR-04), which makes it one way into AP-7 (R-07), and at a clinic no passive sensor sees it (RR-14).
label: Reference work: fictional scenario, not any organization's risk register

title: Tier 0 compromise through the hybrid identity boundary
threat: An attacker with a datacenter foothold harvests directory credentials and abuses the synchronization boundary to control both identity planes
vulnerability: Tier 0 concentration; standing administrator assignments and synchronized privileged accounts in the assumed current state; standing Tier 0 access that no approval gates, which the design keeps for the two emergency access accounts and for Tier 0 workload identities (RR-16)
controls: Cloud-only, unsynchronized administrator accounts; PIM eligible-only, with Tier 0 activation approved by one of two named approvers; PAWs (ADR-004; CA-03 to CA-06); the emergency access exclusion group (grp-ca-emergency-access) as a role-assignable Tier 0 object with no owners (ADR-004 decision 9); emergency access passkeys in split custody at two hospitals, use only from a designated PAW, and validation at least every 90 days that also checks the group's membership (03 section 5); Defender for Identity sensors on domain controllers, AD CS, and Entra Connect servers (PIP-ID-RISK); Protected Users and authentication silos; sealed recovery credentials; detections for Tier 0 credential access and enumeration (DX-05, SG-04), directory replication by hosts or accounts that should not replicate (DX-06, SG-06), Entra Connect server anomalies (DX-07, whose logon and process signals need Defender for Endpoint on the IDS-SYNC servers, which the design does not yet state: threat-model.md TM-A4; until it does, DX-07 rests on its Defender for Identity alert signal), control-plane and trust changes (SN-02), recovery inhibition (DX-01, SN-05), every sign-in by either emergency access account (SN-06), and every change to grp-ca-emergency-access, grp-admins-t0, and grp-admins-t1 and all audit activity by or on the emergency access accounts (SN-07), all untested templates; recovery copies administered outside production Tier 0's reach and monitored as Tier 0 (ADR-009 decisions 2 and 4; requirements only, not designed)
notes: Tier 0 compromise is a full compromise by definition (RR-07). The design removes the synchronized-administrator pivot. Persistence through the emergency access path (AP-5 steps 8a and 8b: joining grp-ca-emergency-access, or resetting an emergency account) needs Tier 0 access first. The emergency accounts and Tier 0 workload identities can make these changes without approval (one emergency account can reset the other, an application granted RoleManagement.ReadWrite.Directory can change the group, and one granted UserAuthMethod-TAP.ReadWrite.All or UserAuthenticationMethod.ReadWrite.All can issue a Temporary Access Pass to either account), so on those paths the alerts (SN-07 for the change, SN-06 for any sign-in it enables) are the only control (RR-16; ADR-004 decision 9; attack-paths.md AP-5). ADR-009 requires that no production Tier 0 credential can delete or alter the recovery copies, which targets the backup deletion at AP-5 step 9; that is a requirement, not a tested capability (RR-11). Recovery decides how Contoso comes back from a Tier 0 compromise, not what the compromise exposed, so the threat model keeps AP-5's impact Critical even after restore tests pass (TM-A1).
label: Reference work: fictional scenario, not any organization's risk register

title: Illicit consent or workload identity abuse reaches ePHI in Microsoft 365
residual_risk_refs: RR-16 (Tier 0 workload identities); workload identity coverage gap
threat: An attacker obtains an application token through illicit consent or a compromised app registration and reads mailboxes and files without a user session
vulnerability: Consent paths that bypass MFA; Conditional Access for workload identities does not cover managed identities or multitenant apps; an application permission is a standing grant that no activation or approval gates, so a Tier 0 workload identity holds standing Tier 0 access (RR-16)
controls: Admin consent workflow and restricted user consent (03 section 6); certificate credentials and no new client secrets (WP-3.6); CA-22 for single-tenant service principals where licensed; no application holds the authentication-method permissions by default, and a grant of a Tier 0 permission needs a Tier 0 administrator or a Tier 0 workload identity, is made against a change record, and raises an alert (03 section 4); the workload identity route, an application that can assign app roles, needs no activation or approval, so on it the alert is the control (RR-16); consent and credential detection SN-03, which scores High a grant of any permission in the 03 section 6 table and any credential added to a Tier 0 workload identity, whoever adds it (untested template); managed identity sign-in monitoring is not built (03 section 6 calls for it; coverage-map.md section 3, item 11); Purview labeling and data loss prevention (phase 3)
notes: SN-03 is written to detect new consents and new application and service principal credentials. Managed identity sign-in monitoring is not built, and neither app-only token sign-ins nor app-only mailbox and file access is detected yet (coverage-map.md sections 3 and 4). RR-16 applies through its workload identity branch: an application or managed identity that holds an application permission able to change a Tier 0 object, or a control Tier 0 depends on, is a Tier 0 workload identity (03 sections 4 and 6). 03 section 6 lists the permissions the design checks for, such as RoleManagement.ReadWrite.Directory and the permissions that can issue a Temporary Access Pass, and says the list is not exhaustive. An AP-6 compromise of one, for example a credential added at step 3, yields standing Tier 0 access that no approval gates. That consequence is a Tier 0 compromise, the impact R-05 scores, so this row does not score it again and its scores still follow AP-6.
label: Reference work: fictional scenario, not any organization's risk register

title: Medical device compromise with availability and data impact
assets: RES-IOMT; PE-NETWORK; PEP-NET-ACCESS; PIP-IOMT-SENSOR; PIP-ASSET-INV; RES-PACS
threat: A compromised or rogue device on a MAC-admitted port uses its allowed flow to reach its device-class server; or a device that cannot encrypt the ePHI it stores is lost or stolen (RR-15)
vulnerability: Unpatchable devices with fixed credentials; MAC-based admission; a single flat biomedical network in the assumed current state; no passive sensor at the 22 clinics (RR-14); device storage that cannot be encrypted (RR-15)
controls: Passive discovery at the three hospital cores and one inventory (PIP-IOMT-SENSOR, PIP-ASSET-INV), with clinic devices classified through NAC profiling and clinical engineering records (RR-14); device-class segments with allow-lists and no lateral traffic (ADR-006); NAC profiling for MAB ports (PE-NETWORK); egress proxy for manufacturer connectivity; clinically gated containment (04 section 3); encryption of stored ePHI where the device supports it, required in new purchase contracts and recorded per device in PIP-ASSET-INV (ADR-006 decision 6); for devices that cannot encrypt, physical safeguards, location records, and media sanitization before disposal, re-use, or return to the manufacturer (RR-15)
treatment: Mitigate; accept the residual with clinical engineering sign-off
notes: Segmentation confines impact to one device class and its server. Containing a device in patient use stays a human decision by design. This row also carries RR-15: a lost or stolen device that cannot encrypt its stored ePHI is a possible breach of unsecured PHI (notification-clocks.md section 2.2). That scenario is judged at or below this row's inherent and residual scores, so it does not raise them and is not scored as a separate risk. Clinic devices get no sensor-based anomaly detection (RR-14). The biomedical vendor variant of AP-3 (R-04) is one way into this path.
label: Reference work: fictional scenario, not any organization's risk register

title: Credential abuse through legacy Kerberos and NTLM paths
threat: Kerberoasting of service accounts, NTLM relay, or abuse of domain controllers published for remote Kerberos single sign-on
vulnerability: Legacy applications that need NTLM; the local plane evaluates fewer signals; remote Kerberos needs a network path to domain controllers
controls: Gateway-enforced enclave with one entry (PEP-ENCLAVE-GW, ADR-005); NTLM audit then restriction with owned, dated exceptions; AES-only Kerberos and group managed service accounts; domain controller segment limited to the groups that need it; Defender for Identity monitoring; retirement plan per application; Kerberoasting detections DX-05 and SG-05 (untested templates)
treatment: Mitigate; avoid over time by retiring legacy applications
notes: Appears as step 6 of AP-4 and step 3 of AP-5. The NTLM timeline is in 04 section 4.
label: Reference work: fictional scenario, not any organization's risk register

title: Insider misuse of legitimate EHR access
threat: An authorized workforce member looks up records without a care relationship, or pulls records in bulk within their role
vulnerability: Zero Trust decides whether a session may exist, not whether each record lookup is appropriate; EHR privacy monitoring is out of scope
controls: Minimum-necessary EHR roles (configuration out of scope); EHR audit logs collected in PIP-SIEM; sanction policy (164.308(a)(1)(ii)(C)); an EHR privacy monitoring program (outside this design)
treatment: Mitigate outside this design (EHR privacy monitoring)
notes: Residual equals inherent on purpose: this design does not reduce the risk.
label: Reference work: fictional scenario, not any organization's risk register

title: Payment terminal tampering or substitution
threat: Criminals swap or tamper with registration-desk terminals to capture card data
vulnerability: Many terminals at registration desks across 3 hospitals and 22 clinics; terminals integrated with workstations in the assumed starting point
controls: Terminals from a PCI-listed P2PE solution that encrypt at the terminal (ADR-007); terminal list in PIP-ASSET-INV; periodic inspection at a frequency set by targeted risk analysis; staff training; PEP-CDE-BOUNDARY isolation; provider management under PCI DSS 12.8
treatment: Mitigate; transfer part to the P2PE provider through written agreements
notes: Card data exposure only, with no ePHI in Z-CDE. The acquirer decides the validation path (A-16).
label: Reference work: fictional scenario, not any organization's risk register

title: Upstream supplier compromise
assets: EXT-VENDOR-EHR; EXT-VENDOR-BIOMED; EXT-PSP; EXT-P2PE; EXT-TELEHEALTH; EXT-RCM-BA
threat: A supplier's environment or software is compromised and affects Contoso's ePHI, payments, or services
vulnerability: Contoso cannot enforce controls inside a supplier
controls: Business associate agreements with security and incident-reporting terms (164.314(a)(2)(i)); third-party service provider management (PCI DSS 12.8.1 to 12.8.5); narrow integrations; full URL redirect instead of embedded payment fields (ADR-007); per-manufacturer egress allow-lists for device connectivity (ADR-006 decision 7); monitoring of supplier access
treatment: Transfer through contracts; mitigate; accept the residual
notes: AP-3 is the access-path form of this risk; this row covers supplier-side compromise more broadly. Biomedical vendors are business associates when their service can reach ePHI on a device, which includes every vendor with broker access (A-13). If a manufacturer's own service is compromised, its allow-listed egress destination gives data on the device a way out that bypasses the broker (attack-paths.md AP-3, biomedical variant).
label: Reference work: fictional scenario, not any organization's risk register

title: Tampering with the patient portal payment redirect
threat: An attacker alters the portal page that starts the payment redirect, or substitutes a counterfeit page for the redirect target, so patients enter card data on a page the attacker controls
vulnerability: The portal sets the redirect target, so whoever can change the page that starts the redirect decides where patients enter card data
controls: Full URL redirect to the payment service provider's hosted page, with no embedded payment fields and only a transaction reference returned (ADR-007, F-11); the page that starts the redirect sits behind PEP-WAF, and its content is change-monitored as defense in depth (ADR-007, 04 section 7); an incident response plan that includes card brand and acquirer notification (04 section 7, notification-clocks.md section 4)
notes: The card-not-present counterpart of R-10, drawn from threat-model.md TB-1 (tampering) and TB-8 (spoofing) rather than an attack path. Compromise at the payment service provider itself is R-11 (RR-12). The portal also holds PHI, so one portal incident can start HIPAA and card brand clocks together (notification-clocks.md section 4). Whether payment page script requirements reach the redirecting page is confirmed with the acquirer or assessor (04 section 7).
label: Reference work: fictional scenario, not any organization's risk register
